modules.title: First conversations
modules.summary: Greet people, thank them, and say who you are.

lessons.title: Hello & thank you
intro: Burmese is spoken with tones: each syllable's pitch, length and voice quality are part of the word. The coloured romanization shows the tone of every syllable (blue low, red high, purple creaky, green checked, grey weak).
Politeness is built into sentence endings. ပါ (bà) softens almost anything, and တယ် (dè) ends a plain statement. You'll hear both all the time.

lessons.title: How are you?
intro: Add လား (lá) to the end of a sentence and it becomes a yes/no question. နေကောင်း means 'to be well', so နေကောင်းလား is literally 'well?'.
Burmese usually drops 'I' and 'you' when it's obvious who you mean.

lessons.title: About me
intro: The polite word for 'I' depends on who's speaking: men say ကျွန်တော် (kyə-nàw), women say ကျွန်မ (kyə-ma̰). Set which one you use in Settings.
Word order is subject, object, verb: the verb always comes last. က (ga̰) after a place means 'from'.

lessons.title: Small talk
intro: A handful of reactions keeps a conversation going even when you understand very little: 'really?', 'good', 'nice to meet you'.

modules.title: The sounds of Burmese
modules.summary: Train your ear for the tones and sounds English doesn't have.

lessons.title: The four tones
intro: Burmese has four tones. They differ in pitch, but also in length and voice quality, so listen for all three.

Low (à): long and level, relaxed. High (á): long, starts high and often falls at the end. Creaky (a̰): short, with a tense, slightly creaky voice. Checked (aʔ): very short, cut off sharply by a catch in the throat.
In the script, ာ alone usually gives low tone, း (two dots) marks high tone, and a bare consonant or ့ (dot below) gives creaky.

lessons.title: Breathy consonants
intro: Burmese separates plain consonants from aspirated ones, said with a puff of air. English has both sounds but never uses the difference to change a word: the p in 'spin' is plain, the p in 'pin' is aspirated.
In romanization an h in front marks the puff: hk, hp, ht, hs.

lessons.title: Breathy nasals
intro: Burmese also has voiceless m, n, ng and l: breathe out through your nose before the sound. They're written hm, hn, hng, hl.
You've already met one: နှစ် (hniʔ) 'two'.

modules.title: When you're stuck
modules.summary: Phrases that rescue a conversation when you're lost.

lessons.title: I don't understand
intro: Negatives wrap the verb: မ (mə) before it and ဘူး (bú) at the end. နားလည် is 'understand', so နားမလည်ဘူး is 'don't understand'.
A verb followed by ပါ (bà) is a polite request: 'please do…'.

lessons.title: What's this called?
intro: Questions with a question word (what, where, how) end in လဲ (lé), not လား. ဘာ (bà) is 'what', ဘယ်လို (bè-lò) is 'how'.
Telling people you're learning usually earns patience and encouragement.

modules.title: Building sentences
modules.summary: A few patterns plus a few verbs let you say hundreds of things.

lessons.title: Everyday verbs
intro: Burmese verbs never change form: no 'go/goes/went'. Time and mood come from small words after the verb.
Learn these ten verbs as building blocks. The next lessons plug them into patterns.

lessons.title: Statements & negatives
intro: Verb + တယ် (dè) is a plain statement, present or past depending on context: သွားတယ် 'I go / I went'.
မ + verb + ဘူး is the negative: မသွားဘူး 'I'm not going / I didn't go'.
After a checked syllable (ending in ʔ), တယ် is said 'tè', without the d sound.

lessons.title: Future & questions
intro: Verb + မယ် (mè) talks about the future or an intention: သွားမယ် 'I'll go'.
Verb + မလား (mə-lá) asks a yes/no question about the future; a question word + verb + မလဲ (mə-lé) asks an open one.

lessons.title: Wanting & asking
intro: Verb + ချင်တယ် (jìn dè) means 'want to'. Verb + ပါ (bà) is a polite request.
ရှိတယ် (shḭ dè) means 'there is' or 'I have'.

modules.title: Food & family
modules.summary: Mealtime phrases and the people around the table.

lessons.title: Have you eaten?
intro: 'Have you eaten?' is a friendly everyday greeting, much like 'how are you?'.
Verb + ပြီးပြီ (pyí bì) means 'already done'.

lessons.title: Mum & dad
intro: အ (ə) at the start of many family words is a weak, unstressed syllable.

lessons.title: One to five
intro: Numbers are worth knowing early: prices, ages, times. Watch the tones: they're what separates similar-sounding numbers.

lessons.title: Six to ten
intro: ခုနစ် 'seven' is written with two syllables but said quickly as one and a half.

modules.title: Questions
modules.summary: Ask who, what, where, when, why, how and how much, and answer simply.

lessons.title: What & who
intro: Almost every Burmese question word is built from ဘာ (bà) 'what' or ဘယ် (bè) 'which'. ဘယ် + သူ 'person' gives ဘယ်သူ (bè-thù) 'who'.
The question word sits where the answer would go, and the sentence ends in လဲ (lé). Yes/no questions end in လား (lá) instead: ချင်လား (jìn lá) 'do you want to…?'.

lessons.title: Where & when
intro: ဘယ်မှာ (bè-hmà) means 'where (at)'. Answer with ဒီမှာ (dì-hmà) 'here' or ဟိုမှာ (hò-hmà) 'over there': same pattern, different first word.
ဘယ်တော့ (bè-da̰w) asks 'when' about the future. For a clock time, ask ဘယ်အချိန် (bè ə-chèin) 'what time'.

lessons.title: Why, how & which
intro: ဘာလို့ (bà-lo̰) is 'why'. To answer 'because…', put လို့ (lo̰) after the reason: အလုပ်များလို့ 'because I'm busy'.
ဘယ်လို (bè-lò) is 'how', and ဘယ်ဟာ (bè-hà) is 'which one'. Handy when someone offers you a choice of dishes.

lessons.title: How much & simple answers
intro: ဘယ်လောက် (bè-lauʔ) is 'how much', for prices and amounts. 'How many' needs a counting word: ယောက် (yauʔ) for people, ခု (hkṵ) for things.
Short answers matter as much as questions. ရှိလား 'is there…?' gets ရှိတယ် 'there is' or မရှိဘူး 'there isn't'. And မသိဘူး 'I don't know' is always allowed.

modules.title: People & family
modules.summary: Brothers, sisters, children and elders, and how to talk to them.

lessons.title: Brothers & sisters
intro: Burmese has no single word for 'brother' or 'sister': it always says older or younger. အစ်ကို (ə-kò) is an older brother, အစ်မ (ə-ma̰) an older sister.
These words are also used to address people a bit older than you, even strangers: calling a young man အစ်ကို is friendly and polite.

lessons.title: Husband, wife & children
intro: သား (thá) is 'son' and သမီး (thə-mí) is 'daughter'. Parents also call their children သား and သမီး directly, like 'son!' or 'sweetheart'.
Questions about marriage and children are normal friendly small talk in Myanmar, not nosy.

lessons.title: This is my…
intro: To introduce someone, say ဒါ (dà) 'this', then the person, then ပါ (bà): ဒါ ကျွန်တော့် အမေပါ 'this is my mother'.
'My' is just 'I' placed before the noun. ကျွန်တော် (men) becomes creaky ကျွန်တော့် (kyə-na̰w); ကျွန်မ (women) stays the same.

lessons.title: Aunty, uncle & age
intro: People rarely use a bare first name. Older women are အန်တီ (àn-tì) 'aunty' and older men ဦးလေး (ú-léi) 'uncle', even if they're not relatives. Many people also call their partner's parents အမေ and အဖေ.
Before a name, ဦး (ú) and ဒေါ် (dàw) show respect to older men and women: ဦးအောင်, ဒေါ်ခင်. For people around your own age, use ကို (kò) for men and မ (ma̰) for women.
Asking someone's age is normal and polite: it tells people which of these words to use.

modules.title: Feelings & health
modules.summary: Say how you feel, and look after someone who isn't well.

lessons.title: Tired & hungry
intro: Feelings are verbs in Burmese, so they take the same endings as any verb: ပင်ပန်းတယ် 'I'm tired', ဗိုက်ဆာလား 'are you hungry?'.
Many feelings are described through the body. ဗိုက် (baiʔ) is 'stomach': a hungry stomach is ဗိုက်ဆာ, a full one ဗိုက်ပြည့်.

lessons.title: Hot, cold & sick
intro: You already know နေကောင်းလား 'how are you?' (literally 'are you well?'). Put it in the negative frame and you have 'I'm not well': နေမကောင်းဘူး.
Aches use the body part + the feeling: ခေါင်း 'head' + ကိုက် 'ache' = a headache.

lessons.title: Are you OK?
intro: အဆင်ပြေလား (ə-hsìn pyèi lá) is the everyday 'are you OK? / is everything alright?'. It works for people, plans and situations.
Burmese families take care of each other out loud: expect to hear 'rest!', 'be careful!' and 'get well soon' a lot. ပါစေ (bà zèi) at the end makes a wish: 'may it be so'.

lessons.title: Happy, sad & bored
intro: စိတ် (seiʔ) means 'mind': many feelings are built on it. စိတ် + ပူ 'hot' = worried, literally a hot mind.
To tell someone not to do something, wrap the verb: မ + verb + ပါနဲ့ (bà nḛ). စိတ်မပူပါနဲ့ 'don't worry'.

modules.title: Numbers & money
modules.summary: Count to ten thousand, ask prices and pay.

lessons.title: Eleven to twenty
intro: Eleven to nineteen are just 'ten + number': ဆယ့်တစ် (hsḛ-tiʔ) is 'ten-one'. Notice ဆယ် 'ten' turns creaky (ဆယ့်) when another number follows it.
Twenty is 'two tens', နှစ်ဆယ်. The 'two' shrinks to a quick, weak hnə, just as 'one' does in တစ်ဆယ် (tə-hsè).

lessons.title: Tens & combining
intro: Tens are 'number + ten'. The ten changes its sound: after an open syllable it's voiced to zè (သုံးဆယ် thóun-zè), after a checked one (ʔ) it stays hsè (ခြောက်ဆယ် chauʔ-hsè).
တစ် 'one', နှစ် 'two' and ခုနစ် 'seven' shrink to weak syllables (tə, hnə, hkṵn-hnə) before ten, hundred and thousand. Bigger numbers are simply stacked: နှစ်ဆယ့်ငါး 'two-ten-five' is 25.

lessons.title: Hundreds & thousands
intro: ရာ (yà) is a hundred, ထောင် (htàun) a thousand and သောင်း (tháun) ten thousand. With kyat, prices run into thousands quickly, so these are the numbers you'll hear most at the market.
When more numbers follow, the bigger unit turns creaky: တစ်ရာ့ငါးဆယ် 150, တစ်ထောင့်ငါးရာ 1,500.

lessons.title: How much is it?
intro: ဘယ်လောက်လဲ (bè-lauʔ lé) 'how much?' works for any price. ဈေး (zéi) means 'price' (and also 'market'): 'price big' is expensive, 'price plentiful' is cheap.
A little friendly bargaining is normal at markets, less so in shops with fixed prices. A smile and နည်းနည်း လျှော့ပေးပါ go a long way.

modules.title: Time & days
modules.summary: Today, tomorrow, days of the week and telling the time.

lessons.title: Today & tomorrow
intro: Time words usually go at the start of the sentence: မနက်ဖြန် သွားမယ် 'tomorrow (I) will go'. Burmese verbs never change, so these words do much of the work English does with tenses.
ဒီ (dì) means 'this': ဒီနေ့ 'this day' is today.

lessons.title: Morning to night
intro: မနက် (mə-neʔ) is the morning, နေ့လည် (nḛ-lè) the middle of the day, ညနေ (nya̰-nèi) late afternoon into evening, and ည (nya̰) night.
Put ဒီ in front again for 'this…': ဒီည 'tonight'.

lessons.title: Days of the week
intro: Day names are said with နေ့ (nḛ, 'day') after them.
The day you were born on matters in Myanmar: it's tied to astrology and often decides the first letter of a person's name. Ask your partner's family which day they were born on!

lessons.title: What time is it?
intro: 'What time is it?' is literally 'how many hours has it become?'. Hours are number + နာရီ (nà-yì): ငါးနာရီ 'five o'clock'. Add ခွဲ (hkwé, 'half') for half past.
Put morning or evening in front to be clear: ညနေ ငါးနာရီ is 5 pm, မနက် ငါးနာရီ 5 am.

modules.title: Counting things
modules.summary: Counter words for people, animals, cups and more.

lessons.title: Counting people
intro: When you count things in Burmese you add a counter word after the number, a bit like 'two cups of…' or 'three head of cattle' in English. The order is noun + number + counter: လူ သုံးယောက် 'person three (counter)' = three people.
ယောက် (yauʔ) counts people. The noun is dropped when it's obvious: just သုံးယောက်ပါ 'three, please'.

lessons.title: Animals & things
intro: ကောင် (kàun) counts animals. ခု (hkṵ) is the general counter for objects: if you're not sure which counter to use, ခု usually works.
The sound changes you met with numbers happen here too: တစ် and နှစ် shrink to tə and hnə, and the counter is often voiced after an open syllable (သုံးခု thóun-gṵ).

lessons.title: Cups, bottles & plates
intro: Drinks are counted by their container: ခွက် (hkweʔ) for cups and glasses, ပုလင်း (bə-lín) for bottles. ပွဲ (pwé) counts servings of food.
To order, say the thing, the amount, then ပေးပါ 'please give': လက်ဖက်ရည် နှစ်ခွက် ပေးပါ. Burmese tea (လက်ဖက်ရည်) is strong, sweet milk tea; the teashop is where people meet and chat.

lessons.title: Round & flat things
intro: လုံး (lóun) counts round things: eggs, fruit, balls. ရွက် (yweʔ) means 'leaf' and counts flat sheets: leaves, paper and banknotes.

modules.title: Food & drink 2
modules.summary: Order at a tea shop, name dishes and tastes, and finish the meal.

lessons.title: At the tea shop
intro: Tea shops are the heart of daily life in Yangon. လက်ဖက်ရည် (lə-hpeʔ-yèi) is the sweet milky tea you order; the pot of plain green tea, ရေနွေးကြမ်း (yèi-nwéi-gyán), sits on the table for free.
To order, name the thing, add how many, then ပေးပါ (péi bà) 'please give'. You call the young waiters ညီလေး (nyì-léi) 'little brother'. It's friendly, not rude.

lessons.title: Dishes
intro: မုန့်ဟင်းခါး (mo̰un-hín-gá), fish noodle soup, is the classic Burmese breakfast.
Meat words end in သား (thá) 'flesh': ကြက် is chicken, so ကြက်သား is chicken meat. ဟင်း (hín) is any curry or dish eaten with rice.

lessons.title: Spicy, sweet, salty, sour
intro: Tastes are verbs in Burmese, so 'it's spicy' is just စပ်တယ် (saʔ tè): taste + တယ်.
Family will often ask if you can handle chilli. နိုင် (nàin) after a verb means 'be able to'.

lessons.title: More, enough & the bill
intro: Hosts keep filling your plate. နည်းနည်း ထပ်ပေးပါ asks for a little more; တော်ပြီ (tàw bì) or ဗိုက်ပြည့်ပြီ politely says you've had enough.
ပြီ (bì) at the end means 'now / already': a change has happened. At a tea shop, say ပိုက်ဆံ ရှင်းမယ် when you want to pay.

modules.title: Getting around
modules.summary: Places, directions and taxi phrases for getting about town.

lessons.title: Places
intro: Learn the places you'll need most. Many are compounds: ဆေး (medicine) + ရုံ (building) = ဆေးရုံ hospital; လေ (air) + ဆိပ် (port) = လေဆိပ် airport.
Notice the sound change: ဆိပ် is hseiʔ on its own but zeiʔ inside လေဆိပ်.

lessons.title: Where is it?
intro: မှာ (hmà) after a word means 'at / in'. ဘယ်မှာ (bè-hmà) is 'where', so 'X where?' is X ဘယ်မှာလဲ.
ဒီ (dì) is 'this', ဟို (hò) is 'that over there': ဒီမှာ 'here', ဟိုမှာ 'over there'.

lessons.title: Left, right, straight
intro: ဘက် (beʔ) means 'side': ဘယ်ဘက် left side, ညာဘက် right side. Careful: ဘယ် also means 'which / where', and the context tells you which.
Add a verb + ပါ to give directions politely: ကွေ့ပါ 'please turn', သွားပါ 'please go'.

lessons.title: Taking a taxi
intro: Yangon taxis usually have no meter, so agree the price before you get in: say where you're going, then ask ဘယ်လောက်လဲ 'how much?'.
ကို (gò) after a place marks where you're going: ဈေးကို သွားမယ် 'I'll go to the market'.

modules.title: Daily life
modules.summary: Talk about your day, what you're doing, and whether you're busy.

lessons.title: Morning to night
intro: Time words go at the start of the sentence: မနက် ရေချိုးတယ် 'In the morning I shower'.
There are new verbs here. Try them with the patterns you know: နိုးတယ် 'I woke up', နိုးပြီးပြီ 'I'm already up'.

lessons.title: At home
intro: Verb + နေ (nèi) means you're in the middle of doing something, like English '-ing': ချက်နေတယ် 'I'm cooking'.
ကြည့် (kyḭ) 'look' also means 'watch', so watching TV is တီဗွီ ကြည့် (tì-bwì kyḭ).

lessons.title: Work & study
intro: အလုပ် (ə-louʔ) is 'work, a job'. It comes from လုပ် 'do', which you already know, so 'I'm working' is အလုပ်လုပ်နေတယ်.
ပြန် (pyàn) means 'go back, return'. With အိမ် 'home' it's how you say you're heading home.

lessons.title: Busy or free?
intro: ဘာလုပ်နေလဲ 'what are you doing?' is how many phone calls start.
အား (á) means 'to have free time'. So အားလား is 'are you free?', and မအားဘူး 'not free' is the usual way to say you're busy.

modules.title: Past & plans
modules.summary: Say what you did, what you will do, what you must and can do.

lessons.title: Did it, done it, not yet
intro: Plain verb + တယ် can already mean past, and time words like မနေ့က 'yesterday' usually do the work. To make the past clear, add ခဲ့ (gḛ): သွားခဲ့တယ် 'I went'.
Verb + ပြီးပြီ (pyí bì) means 'already done'. For 'not yet', wrap the verb in မ … သေးဘူး: မစားရသေးဘူး 'I haven't eaten yet'.

lessons.title: Plans & must
intro: You already know မယ် (mè) for the future and ချင်တယ် (jìn dè) for 'want to'. Add တော့ before မယ် for 'about to, right now': စားတော့မယ် 'I'm going to eat now'.
ရ (ya̰) after a verb means 'have to': သွားရမယ် 'I have to go'. Say it when you need to leave a family visit.

lessons.title: Have you ever…?
intro: ဖူး (hpú) after a verb means 'have ever done'. ရောက်ဖူးလား 'have you ever been (there)?' is a favourite question for visitors.
For 'never', use the usual negative: မ + verb + ဖူးဘူး. After an open syllable ဖူး usually sounds like bú.

lessons.title: Can & can't
intro: Burmese has two words for 'can'. နိုင် (nàin) is being able to or having the chance: လာနိုင်တယ် 'I can come'. တတ် (daʔ) is a learned skill: ရေကူးတတ်တယ် 'I can swim'.
To ask permission, use verb + လို့ရလား: ထိုင်လို့ရလား 'Can I sit?'

modules.title: Opinions & small talk
modules.summary: Share what you think, react, compliment the food and chat about the weather.

lessons.title: I think, I like
intro: ထင်တယ် (htìn dè) 'I think' goes at the end, after the opinion: ကောင်းမယ် ထင်တယ် 'I think it'll be good'.
ကြိုက်တယ် is 'like'. Put အရမ်း (ə-yán) 'very' in front to make it stronger.

lessons.title: Good, beautiful, fun
intro: Describing words work like verbs: လှတယ် 'is beautiful', ကောင်းတယ် 'is good'. Make them negative the same way: မကောင်းဘူး 'not good'.
စရာကောင်းတယ် after a verb means 'worth doing': ပျော်စရာကောင်းတယ် 'it's fun'.

lessons.title: Me too & agreeing
intro: လည်း (lé) after a word means 'too, also': ကျွန်မလည်း ကြိုက်တယ် 'I like it too'.
Burmese conversation avoids flat disagreement. မထင်ဘူး 'I don't think so' or ဖြစ်နိုင်တယ် 'maybe' are gentle ways to disagree.

lessons.title: Compliments & weather
intro: Praising the food is the best compliment you can give at a family meal. Say it often!
Weather is easy small talk: Yangon is usually hot or rainy. ဒီနေ့ 'today' + အရမ်းပူတယ် 'really hot' will always get a reply.

scriptModules.title: Consonants
scriptModules.summary: The alphabet, row by row, with the pattern that ties it together.

lessons.title: How the script works
intro: Burmese letters are built from circles and curves. It was traditionally written by scratching palm leaves, where straight lines would split the leaf. So look closely at where each circle opens, and what's added to it: a tail, a second loop, a gap.
Every consonant comes with a built-in short 'a' sound (creaky tone). On its own, မ is 'ma̰', not just 'm'. Vowels and tones are small marks added around it.
Each letter gets a memory hook: a word you already know from the course.

lessons.title: The sound grid: throat row
intro: Here's the big shortcut: most consonants sit in a grid. Each ROW is a place in your mouth (throat, palate, teeth, lips). The COLUMNS go: plain, breathy (with a puff of air), voiced, voiced (a rare spelling), and nasal.
Learn the pattern once and every row makes sense. This row is made in the throat: k, hk, g, (g), ng.
The rare 4th-column letters mostly appear in religious or Pali words, so we skip them for now.

lessons.title: Palate row
intro: Same pattern, further forward in the mouth: s, hs, z, ny.
Breathy partners again: စ (s) and ဆ (hs) differ only in the puff of air.

lessons.title: Teeth row
intro: Tongue on the teeth: t, ht, d, n.
တ (t) and ထ (ht) are partners: notice how often you've already seen both, in တယ် and ထမင်း.

lessons.title: Lips row
intro: Lips: p, hp, b, b, m. This row's two voiced letters are both used, and both say 'b'.
You now know the whole grid pattern.

lessons.title: The rest
intro: These sit outside the grid: y, y (spelled r), l, w, th, h, and the vowel carrier အ.
ရ is a classic trap: it's spelled 'r' but said 'y' in Yangon. You'll see it in ရေ (water).

scriptModules.title: Vowels & tones
scriptModules.summary: Marks around a letter set the vowel and the tone.

lessons.title: Long a & the high dots
intro: ာ after a consonant gives a long 'a' in low tone.
The two dots း always push a syllable to HIGH tone: the dots sit up high. Same letter, same vowel, different word: ကာ vs ကား (car).

lessons.title: i and u
intro: Marks above and below: a small circle on top is 'i', a hook below is 'u'.
The short versions (ိ ု) are creaky; the long versions (ီ ူ) are low; add း for high.

lessons.title: The vowel written first
intro: ေ is the famous trick of Burmese script: you WRITE it before the consonant, but SAY it after. ကေ is k + ei.
ဲ is 'e' as in 'bed', and it's high tone on its own. Add a dot below (့) and any syllable becomes creaky (squeezed).

lessons.title: Lego vowels
intro: Some vowels are two marks combined: ေ + ာ = 'aw', and ိ + ု = 'o'.
Then the same tone marks apply: း for high, ် to make 'aw' low.

scriptModules.title: Endings & stacks
scriptModules.summary: Final sounds, and letters that attach to others.

lessons.title: The killer mark
intro: The small mark ် on top 'kills' a letter's own vowel, so it becomes an ending.
Rule of thumb: a STOP letter at the end (က် တ် ပ် စ်) = a sharp cut-off (checked tone, ʔ). A NASAL letter at the end (င် န် မ်) = the vowel goes nasal.

lessons.title: Letters that attach
intro: Four marks hook onto a consonant to change it: ျ and ြ add a 'y' (in Yangon they sound the same), ွ adds a 'w', and ှ makes it breathy.
You've met them already: ကျေးဇူး, ဖြည်းဖြည်း, သွား, နှစ်.

lessons.title: Read real words
intro: Put it together: these are words from your speaking lessons. Sound them out letter by letter before you check.

scriptModules.title: Reading practice
scriptModules.summary: Read real words and phrases from each speaking module.

lessons.title: Read: Questions
intro: Question words all start with ဘ: spot ဘာ 'what' and ဘယ် 'which' at the front, and လဲ or လား at the end.

lessons.title: Read: Family
intro: Many family words start with the vowel carrier အ. Look for the letter that follows it: ကို, မ, ဖွား, ဘိုး.

lessons.title: Read: Feelings
intro: Feelings are verbs, so most of these end in တယ်. Read the word in front of it to find the feeling.

lessons.title: Read: Numbers & money
intro: Prices on market signs are usually written in Burmese digits (၁၀၀၀ = 1,000), but you'll also see numbers spelled out. Look for ဆယ်, ရာ and ထောင်: the shape of each tells you the size of the number.

lessons.title: Read: Time & days
intro: နေ့ 'day' appears in lots of time words: ဒီနေ့, မနေ့က, and every day of the week. Spot it first, then read the rest.

lessons.title: Read: Counting things
intro: Counters are short, common words, so they're good reading practice. Find the number in each phrase; the counter is the syllable right after it.

lessons.title: Read: Food & drink
intro: Tea-shop and kitchen words. Look for သား (meat) at the end of the meat words.

lessons.title: Read: Places
intro: Places around town. Spot အိမ် (home) inside အိမ်သာ (toilet).

lessons.title: Read: Daily life
intro: Short words for times of day and new verbs. Several are a single syllable.

lessons.title: Read: Past & plans
intro: Look for the little words after the verb: ခဲ့ (past), ပြီ (already), ရ (must), နိုင် (can), ဖူး (ever).

lessons.title: Read: Opinions & small talk
intro: Short sentences you'll say at every family meal. Spot the negative frame မ … ဘူး.
